fixes.explanation: Right, the message says, "Do not rejoice, all you Philistines, that the rod that struck you is broken." (Isaiah 14:29) It tells them not to rejoice. A broken rod sounds like a party with balloons, but the message has more to say. Keep that confetti in the closet, friend.

You've got it, baker. The message says, "…a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg." (Isaiah 14:29) So the snake's root isn't done producing trouble. A viper is a venomous snake, and the verse names a flying serpent too. That is a LOT of snake news for one verse.

A lion is a solid guess, friend, since lions are famous for being scary. But the message stays with snakes here. It says, "…a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg." (Isaiah 14:29) The answer is a viper, and the verse names a flying serpent too.

A bear is a big guess, baker. But the message keeps this one in the snake family. It says, "…a viper will spring from the root of the snake, and a flying serpent from its egg." (Isaiah 14:29) So the answer is a viper, and no bears are invited.

Not quite, friend. The message says, "Then the firstborn of the poor will find pasture, and the needy will lie down in safety…" (Isaiah 14:30) So the firstborn of the poor find pasture, and the needy lie down in safety. Both of those are in the verse, and I'm happy about it.
Yes, baker. The message says, "…I will kill your root by famine…" (Isaiah 14:30) This is a heavy line. The root is what a plant grows from, and here it is the Philistines' root that is named.
